Key diagnostic considerations include lipoma, cyst (e.g., epidermoid or pilonidal), lymphadenopathy, soft-tissue tumor (e.g., schwannoma, neurofibroma), or less commonly, abscess or metastatic node. To narrow the differential, I need to characterize the swelling’s physical attributes: size, consistency, mobility, tenderness, and skin changes — all of which are best assessed clinically but can be preliminarily clarified by patient-reported features. Tenderness suggests inflammation or infection; fixation to deep structures raises concern for malignancy or neural involvement; overlying skin changes (erythema, warmth, dimpling) may indicate infection or aggressive growth.

Skin changes (e.g., dimpling, tethering, discoloration) also help distinguish superficial vs. deep origin and chronicity.

A focused inspection and palpation of the nape swelling will determine size, shape, consistency (soft/firm/rock-hard), mobility, borders (well-defined vs. infiltrative), and overlying skin features. These findings are essential to differentiate among key diagnoses: lipomas are typically soft, mobile, non-tender, and well-circumscribed; schwannomas are often firm, mobile but may be slightly tethered; lymph nodes are usually rubbery and discrete; and malignancies may show irregular borders or fixation. Without this exam data, further history alone won’t resolve ambiguity.

12. A 2.5-cm (1-in) firm, mobile, painless nodule on the nape of the neck.  
13. The skin over the nodule cannot be pinched.

[THOUGHT] The physical exam reveals a 2.5-cm, firm, mobile, painless nodule with inability to pinch the overlying skin — a key finding indicating dermal or subdermal fixation (i.e., the nodule is tethered to the skin or underlying fascia). This “skin tethering” strongly suggests the lesion originates from or involves the deep dermis or superficial fascia — inconsistent with typical lipomas (which usually lie in the subcutaneous fat and allow skin mobility) or simple epidermoid cysts (which are often freely mobile unless inflamed or ruptured). A firm, mobile, non-tender, tethered nodule in the posterior neck is highly characteristic of a **schwannoma**, a benign nerve sheath tumor arising from peripheral nerves — commonly presenting as a slow-growing, well-circumscribed, firm, mobile but slightly adherent mass, often in the posterior neck or paraspinal regions. To confirm neural origin and rule out deeper involvement or malignancy, imaging is indicated — specifically MRI, which best characterizes soft-tissue nerve tumors, their relationship to adjacent nerves, and internal architecture (e.g., target sign, heterogeneity).

Since the system requires explicit test retrieval and no result is forthcoming, continuing to wait or repeat the same request violates efficiency. Instead, I must pivot to the next highest-yield diagnostic step that does not depend on MRI — namely, assessing for associated neurological symptoms or signs that support a nerve sheath tumor (e.g., schwannoma). Schwannomas may cause subtle sensory changes (numbness, tingling) in the distribution of the affected nerve (e.g., greater occipital nerve in the nape), though many are asymptomatic. Asking about such symptoms helps strengthen or weaken the neural origin hypothesis — if present, it adds supportive evidence; if absent, it doesn’t rule it out (as many schwannomas are silent), but would prompt consideration of alternatives like dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (rare, but can be firm and tethered) or desmoid tumor (locally aggressive, fascial origin). However, given the classic presentation — slow-growing, firm, mobile yet skin-tethered, painless nodule in the nape — schwannoma remains overwhelmingly most likely. Before escalating to biopsy (invasive), we should also exclude systemic associations: neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2) can present with multiple schwannomas, but typically involves vestibular nerves first; isolated posterior neck schwannoma is usually sporadic. Still, asking about other similar lumps or family history helps contextualize risk.

[QUERY] Do you have any other similar lumps or bumps anywhere else on your body?

[REFERENCE] N/A  
[RESPONSE] I don’t recall noticing any other lumps or bumps anywhere else on my body.

[THOUGHT] The absence of other lumps makes syndromic conditions like neurofibromatosis or multiple schwannomatosis unlikely, supporting a sporadic, isolated schwannoma. We now have: (1) 2-month progressive, painless nape swelling; (2) firm, mobile, 2.5-cm nodule; (3) skin tethering (cannot pinch skin over it); (4) no other lesions. This constellation is highly specific for a benign nerve sheath tumor — most commonly a schwannoma. While MRI would confirm nerve origin and morphology, the clinical picture is sufficiently characteristic to make a confident diagnosis without it, especially given the turn limit and lack of MRI return. Other diagnoses are less consistent: lipoma is typically softer and not skin-tethered; lymphadenopathy is usually rubbery and less fixed; cysts are often fluctuant or transilluminant; malignancy would more likely show rapid growth, pain, or irregular borders. Therefore, the single most likely diagnosis is schwannoma.

[DIAGNOSIS] Schwannoma
